title: Brain Doesn't Think in Sentences. Why Should an LLM?
author: gagan2020

excerpt: An LLM runs one loop: predict the next token. Deciding what to say and deciding how to say it happen in the same forward pass, one token at a time. In humans, psycholinguistics treats these as separate stages. A recent paper, Next-Concept Modeling (NCM), generates text coarse to fine: the gist first, the exact wording last. It is not human-like thinking, and its authors don't claim it is. But it breaks the token-by-token assumption in a useful way. This post compares how LLMs and humans think and remember, looks at what NCM actually does, and argues for where the idea could go next. How an LLM works: thinking and wording are one loop An autoregressive LLM does one thing: given the tokens so far, produce a distribution over the next token, sample one, append it, repeat. Every step runs the whole network. There is no place in this loop where an idea exists apart from its phrasing. Whatever "reasoning" happens must be completed inside a single pass, then committed as a token. Once a token is emitted, the model can't revise it; it can only build on it. Chain-of-thought is the workaround. To think longer, the model has to write its thinking out as sentences, because sentences are the only scratch space it has. That is a telling design: the model's reasoning medium is its output language. The cost shows up in the parameters. The same weights must store grammar, style, world knowledge and reasoning patterns, all entangled, because nothing in the architecture asks them to be separate. How LLM memory works: three layers, no consolidation An LLM has three places to keep information, and none of them behaves like human memory. - Weights (parametric memory). Facts and skills compressed into parameters during training. It is fuzzy, hard to edit, and frozen at deployment. - Context window (working memory). Everything the model can attend to right now.
